name: Catharsis
aliases: The catharsis of pity and fear
statement: Tragedy's cleansing of the emotions: the purgation, purification, or clarification of pity and fear.
statementAccent: the purgation, purification, or clarification of pity and fear
meaning: Catharsis, from the Greek katharsis meaning cleansing, purgation, or purification, is a concept from Aristotle's Poetics concerning the effect of tragedy on its audience. In his famous definition, Aristotle characterizes tragedy as an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude, which through pity and fear effects the catharsis of these emotions. So watching a tragedy arouses pity and fear and brings about their catharsis. The great difficulty is that Aristotle nowhere clearly explains in the Poetics what catharsis is; he mentions it essentially once, in the definition of tragedy, and refers to a fuller treatment elsewhere, possibly in the lost second book of the Poetics, so its meaning has been famously disputed for centuries. Three main interpretations compete. On the purgation reading, drawing on a medical metaphor, tragedy purges, discharges, or relieves the built-up emotions of pity and fear, a kind of homeopathic emotional release that leaves the spectator calmer. On the purification reading, drawing on a religious or ritual metaphor, the emotions themselves are refined, purified, or clarified and educated, so that we come to feel pity and fear at the right things. On the clarification reading, associated with modern scholars such as Leon Golden, catharsis is a cognitive clarification, an understanding of the events that arouse pity and fear, yielding learning and its attendant pleasure. Catharsis is central to the paradox of tragedy and is often read as Aristotle's defense of tragedy against Plato.
mechanism: Catharsis names whatever it is that tragic drama does to the emotions of pity and fear that it arouses, and the competing interpretations spell out the mechanism differently because Aristotle left it unexplained. The tragedy first arouses the emotions: through the representation of a serious action in which a person of stature suffers a reversal, the audience is moved to pity for the sufferer and fear for themselves or for humanity. What then happens to these aroused emotions is the crux. The purgation interpretation, drawing on the medical sense of katharsis as the evacuation of harmful matter, takes tragedy to discharge or flush out an excess of pity and fear, relieving emotional pressure and restoring a healthy equilibrium, so that the spectator leaves lighter and calmer, as if the feelings had been drained off. The purification interpretation takes catharsis to refine rather than remove the emotions, correcting excess and deficiency so that we come to feel pity and fear in the right measure and toward the right objects, an ethical and emotional education that habituates virtuous responsiveness. The clarification interpretation locates the effect in the understanding: by representing why the tragic events occur, the drama removes obscurities and clarifies the universal patterns of pity- and fear-arousing action, so that the audience learns something, and the characteristic pleasure of tragedy is the pleasure of this learning. On any reading, catharsis is offered as a positive effect that makes tragedy valuable rather than harmful, and it is widely understood as Aristotle's response to Plato's charge, in the Republic, that tragic poetry harmfully feeds and waters the irrational emotions.

examples.text: Aristotle defined tragedy as an imitation of a serious action that, through pity and fear, effects the catharsis of these emotions.
Catharsis is read as purging the emotions of pity and fear, or as purifying and educating them to the right measure.
Catharsis is often read as Aristotle's defense of tragedy against Plato's charge that it feeds the irrational emotions.

variants.name: Purgation, purification, clarification
variants.text: The three main readings of catharsis: medical discharge of emotion, ethical refinement, and cognitive clarification.

variants.name: The later therapeutic use
variants.text: The distinct, much later adoption of catharsis in psychology and psychoanalysis for emotional release in therapy.

whyItMatters: Catharsis is one of the most famous and contested concepts in the history of aesthetics and literary theory, and it lies at the heart of Aristotle's Poetics, the founding text of Western literary criticism. Because Aristotle attaches catharsis to the very definition of tragedy, understanding it promises to reveal what tragedy is for and why it has value, and the centuries of debate over its meaning, purgation, purification, or clarification, amount to a long inquiry into the relation between art and the emotions. Catharsis is central to the paradox of tragedy, the puzzle of why audiences take pleasure in art that arouses painful feelings, since it offers one traditional answer: that tragedy does something beneficial with the pity and fear it evokes, whether relieving, refining, or clarifying them. It is also pivotal to the ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry, standardly read as Aristotle's reply to Plato's charge that tragic poetry corrupts the soul by feeding the passions. The term later took on a distinct life in psychology, in Freud and Breuer's cathartic method and the wider idea of emotional release.

working.text: let tragedy move the audience to pity for the sufferer and fear for themselves through a serious action.
effect their catharsis, whether by purging, purifying, or clarifying the pity and fear.
leave the spectator relieved, morally refined, or enlightened, making tragedy valuable rather than harmful.

limits: Catharsis is genuinely obscure, and its meaning cannot be settled with certainty from Aristotle's text. He mentions it only once in the surviving Poetics, in the definition of tragedy, and never explains it, so every interpretation is a reconstruction, and the three main readings, purgation, purification, and clarification, each have textual and philosophical support without any commanding consensus. The purgation reading rests on a medical metaphor Aristotle does not develop; the purification reading fits his ethics but reads much into a single word; the clarification reading, associated with Leon Golden and connected by others such as Martha Nussbaum to the removal of obscurities, is attractive but modern. The idea that a fuller account appeared in a lost second book of the Poetics is a plausible scholarly inference rather than an established fact. The exact wording of the definition varies across translations, so it should be attributed to the Poetics generally rather than to a single canonical quotation. And the later psychological use of catharsis, in Freud and Breuer, is a distinct development that should not be read back into Aristotle.
misreadings: Catharsis is not clearly defined by Aristotle, so no single interpretation, purgation, purification, or clarification, can be asserted as certainly his; the concept is genuinely contested. It is not the same as the later psychoanalytic notion of emotional release, which borrows the word but is a distinct development. And it is not simply the venting of feeling, since the purification and clarification readings take it to refine or enlighten rather than merely discharge, so treating catharsis as definitely meaning purgation, as identical to the Freudian sense, or as mere emotional release, misreads Aristotle's concept.
origin: The concept from Aristotle's Poetics that tragedy, through arousing pity and fear, effects their catharsis, variously interpreted as purgation, purification, or clarification, and left unexplained by Aristotle.

sources.text: Aristotle's Aesthetics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — catharsis as the most enigmatic term of the Poetics, effected by tragedy through pity and fear, Aristotle's failure to define it explicitly, and the contested purgation, purification, and clarification interpretations.

Catharsis, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — catharsis in Aristotle's Poetics as the purgation or purification of the emotions of pity and fear aroused by tragedy, and its later use in criticism and psychology.
